books.section: Topic 4.7 Expanding Democracy, A. Participatory Democracy and an Expanding Electorate

stimulus.text:
The table shows the share of eligible voters who cast ballots in presidential elections, 
from 1824 to 1840, as recorded by the U.S. Bureau of the Census.
| Year | Share of eligible voters who voted |
| 1824 | 26.9% |
| 1828 | 57.6% |
| 1832 | 55.4% |
| 1836 | 57.8% |
| 1840 | 80.2% |
stimulus.source_note: U.S. Bureau of the Census, Historical Statistics of the United States, Colonial Times to 1970. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus as described in the stimulus source note
stem: Which claim about the years 1832 to 1836 does the table best support?

options.text: Turnout fell back to its 1824 level
options.misconception: Turnout stayed above 55 percent, more than double the 1824 figure.

options.text: High turnout held steady once the expanded electorate was in place
Turnout doubled again between the elections of 1832 and 1836
options.misconception: It moved only from 55.4 to 57.8 percent, a small rise, not a doubling.

options.text: The Bank War ended mass voting
options.misconception: Turnout stayed high through the Bank War years; the table shows no collapse.

rationales.A: Turnout stayed above 55 percent, far above the 1824 level.
rationales.B: Turnout stayed near 55 to 58 percent in 1832 and 1836, so the 1828 surge lasted instead of fading.
rationales.C: The rise from 55.4 to 57.8 percent is small, not a doubling.
rationales.D: The table shows high turnout through the Bank War years.
rationales.general:
1. Compare the middle years. The table gives 55.4 percent for 1832 and 57.8 percent for 1836.
2. Set them against 1824. Both are more than double the 26.9 percent of 1824.
3. Name the pattern. A surge that holds for two more elections is a new normal, not a one-year spike.
Background: The 1840 jump to 80.2 percent came when both parties ran full mass campaigns.
Remember: a flat line after a jump tells you the change stuck.
